design.whole_content_draft: One succession governs planetary hours continuously through day and night. A day takes the ruler of its first hour. Advancing through twenty-four hours therefore advances three places in the seven-member succession. An alternative skip-two calculation yields the same following day ruler, and the two descriptions must agree. No target word or paragraph is equated with one hour, one day or one position in a seven-item list.
coupled_claims: One fixed seven-member succession continues hourly through day and night.
The first hour’s ruler names or governs that day.
A complete day-night span has twenty-four hourly positions, so the next day ruler is obtained by the same hourly successor applied twenty-four times.

semantic_consequence.hourly_order: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon, then repeat. This is source-owned content, not target-assigned names.
semantic_consequence.modern_relation: Let H be that successor cycle and D the day successor. H^7=id and D=H^24=H^3. Repeatedly skipping two intermediate members gives the same D.
semantic_consequence.joint_consequence: The first-hour ruler after a full day must agree with the skip-two derivation. A list with D=H still cycles through all seven members but predicts the wrong next day ruler.
semantic_consequence.source_written_example: Main text gives first-day Saturn, second-day Sun and third-day Moon; full daily cycle is also in the edition’s explanatory note. No target name is identified.
semantic_consequence.prospective_target_consequence: The same ruler argument must survive both an hour-based derivation and a day-based conclusion. Merely finding two repeated families or seven words would not establish the relation.
semantic_consequence.symmetry: Cyclic phase, simultaneous reversal of H and D, and global relabeling preserve the abstract relation. The equation alone cannot identify natural planet names or an absolute weekday.

concrete_rivals: Independent hourly and daily lists can each have period seven while violating D=H^3.
Resetting the hourly sequence to the same first planet every morning produces a constant daily ruler.
Using only daylight and silently dropping the night changes the count used by the two derivations; a fixed day-night scope is required.
